title: RecExplainer: Aligning Large Language Models for Explaining Recommendation Models

problem.claim: Embedding-based recommender models often operate as black boxes, reducing transparency and reliability for users and developers.

gap.claim: The paper explores using large language models as surrogate models for explaining black-box recommender models.

contributions.claim: The approach trains large language models to comprehend and emulate the behavior of target recommender models.
The paper introduces behavior alignment, intention alignment, and hybrid alignment for aligning large language models with recommendation models.
The aligned language-model surrogate uses natural language to produce customizable explanations adaptable to individual user preferences.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on three public datasets reportedly show promising performance in understanding and mimicking target models, with high-quality, high-fidelity, and distinct explanations.

narrative_sequence.summary: Recommender systems and expressive embedding-based models are widely used, but the models can be opaque.
The paper proposes aligning large language models as surrogate models that emulate recommender behavior and support explanation.
Three alignment strategies operate in language space, latent space, or both.
Experiments on three public datasets report promising model understanding, mimicry, and explanation quality.

source_observation.claim: A language model can be aligned with a black-box recommender through behavioral, latent-intention, or hybrid representations.

interpretation.claim: Explanation quality may depend on which aspects of model behavior are exposed to the surrogate.

application.claim: For opaque recommendation systems, compare language-space, latent-space, and combined alignment strategies when designing explanation interfaces.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which alignment strategy performs best or under what conditions.

unknowns: The abstract omits quantitative metrics, baselines, and detailed experimental results.
The abstract omits training procedures, model configurations, dataset identities, and limitations.
